front: Ray optics and its two basic phenomena
back: Ray optics treats light as travelling along straight lines (rays) and explains reflection, refraction, total internal reflection, dispersion and image formation by mirrors, lenses and prisms. Its two basic phenomena are reflection (ray bounces back into the same medium) and refraction (ray bends as it crosses into another medium).
(1) The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, i = r. (2) The incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal to the surface at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane.

All distances are measured from the pole of the mirror or the optical centre of the lens. Distances measured in the direction of the incident light are positive, those measured against it are negative. Heights measured upward from the principal axis are positive, heights downward negative.

front: Focal length of a spherical mirror
back: f = R/2, where R is the radius of curvature. The concave mirror has f negative, the convex mirror f positive. The relation is derived for paraxial rays only.
1/v + 1/u = 1/f, valid for concave and convex mirrors, real and virtual images. m = h'/h = -v/u. A negative m means a real inverted image, a positive m a virtual erect image.

front: Image formed by a concave mirror, object between P and F
back: The image is behind the mirror, virtual, erect and enlarged, with m > 1. This is the magnifying-mirror (shaving mirror) case. When the object is exactly at F the reflected rays are parallel and the image is at infinity.

front: Image formed by a convex mirror
back: For every object position the image is virtual, erect and diminished, and lies between the pole and the focus - hence its use as a wide-angle rear-view mirror. The proof follows from 1/v = 1/f - 1/u with f > 0 and u < 0, which makes v always positive and m = f/(x + f) < 1.

front: Uses of concave and convex mirrors
back: Concave: shaving/make-up mirror, dentists' mirror, headlights and searchlights (source at focus gives a parallel beam), solar furnaces. Convex: rear-view mirrors of vehicles, blind-corner mirrors - because the field of view is much wider.

front: Snell's law and relative refractive index
back: n21 = sin i / sin r = v1 / v2, where n21 is the refractive index of medium 2 with respect to medium 1, and the absolute refractive index is n = c/v. Light bends towards the normal in an optically denser medium (n21 > 1, r < i) and away from it in a rarer one.

Optical density is measured by the refractive index, i.e. it records the speed of light in the medium; mass density is mass per unit volume. They need not agree - turpentine is optically denser than water but has a lower mass density.
Air 1.0003, ice 1.31, water 1.33, fused quartz 1.46, crown glass 1.52, Canada balsam 1.53, dense flint glass 1.65, ruby 1.71, sapphire 1.77, diamond 2.42.

front: Shift produced by a glass slab
back: A ray passing through a parallel-sided slab emerges parallel to its original direction, laterally displaced. For an object viewed through the slab the apparent shift is t(1 - 1/n); for a slab thickness 15 cm and n = 1.5 the shift is 5 cm, independent of where the slab sits.

front: Total internal reflection and critical angle
back: TIR requires light travelling from an optically denser to a rarer medium with the angle of incidence exceeding the critical angle. At the critical angle the refracted ray grazes the surface, so sin i_c = n21, where n21 is the refractive index of the rarer medium with respect to the denser. Beyond it Snell's law has no solution and all light is reflected.

Water-air 48.75 degrees, crown glass-air 41.14 degrees, dense flint glass-air 37.31 degrees, diamond-air 24.41 degrees. A high refractive index gives a small critical angle, which is why a diamond sparkles and finds use in total-internal-reflection prisms.

Optical fibres (core denser than cladding; used in endoscopy, telecommunications), totally reflecting prisms in binoculars and periscopes (90-degree and 180-degree turns), the mirage, and the sparkling of diamond, cut so that light strikes inner faces beyond i_c.

A right-angled isosceles prism struck normally on one face sends the ray to the hypotenuse at 45 degrees; total internal reflection there turns it through 90 degrees. This needs i_c < 45 degrees, satisfied by crown glass (41.1 degrees) and dense flint glass (37.3 degrees). Illuminating the hypotenuse gives a 180-degree turn and an inverted image of the same size.

front: Refraction at a single spherical surface
back: n2/v - n1/u = (n2 - n1)/R, where n1 and n2 are the refractive indices of the two media and R the radius of curvature. It follows from n1/OM + n2/MI = (n2 - n1)/MC using the sign convention.

1/f = (n2/n1 - 1)(1/R1 - 1/R2). For a lens in air this is 1/f = (n - 1)(1/R1 - 1/R2). R1 is positive and R2 negative for a biconvex lens (giving f > 0); for a biconcave lens R1 is negative and R2 positive, giving f < 0.

1/v - 1/u = 1/f, with m = h'/h = v/u. Note the lens equation has a minus sign before 1/u and the lens magnification no minus sign, unlike the mirror forms. A virtual object (converging beam meeting behind the lens) has u positive.

front: Power of a lens and combinations
back: P = 1/f with f in metres; the SI unit is the dioptre, 1 D = 1 m^-1. P is positive for a converging lens and negative for a diverging one. For thin lenses in contact P = P1 + P2 + P3 + ..., the algebraic sum, and the total magnification is m1 m2 m3 ...

front: Prism: deviation in terms of angles
back: For a prism of refracting angle A with angles of incidence i and emergence e, r1 + r2 = A and delta = (i - r1) + (e - r2) = i + e - A. The deviation grows with i up to a minimum and then increases again.

front: Minimum deviation and refractive index of a prism
back: At minimum deviation the ray inside the prism is parallel to the base, i = e and r1 = r2 = A/2. Then delta = Dm = 2i - A, so i = (A + Dm)/2, and n21 = sin[(A + Dm)/2] / sin(A/2). For a thin prism Dm = (n21 - 1)A.

White light splits because the refractive index of glass falls with increasing wavelength. Red has the smallest n, so it is deviated least; violet has the largest n and is deviated most. The angular spread between the two extremes is the angular dispersion, and a second, inverted prism can recombine the colours.

front: Scattering of light and its wavelength dependence
back: Scattering by particles much smaller than the wavelength varies as 1/lambda^4. Blue is therefore scattered out of sunlight far more than red, so the sky looks blue and the setting Sun looks red. Large particles scatter all wavelengths nearly equally, which is why clouds and fog look white.

A single convex lens of short focal length held close to the eye with the object just inside F. With the image at the near point D, m = 1 + D/f; with the image at infinity, m = D/f. Realistic focal lengths give m of about 6 to 9, so a simple microscope is limited.

The objective (small f_o, small aperture) forms a real, inverted, magnified image, which the eyepiece (small f_e) magnifies further. With the final image at infinity m = (L/f_o)(D/f_e), where L is the tube length between the second focal point of the objective and the first focal point of the eyepiece. Magnifications multiply, so much larger values than a simple microscope are possible.

Objective of large focal length f_o and large aperture, eyepiece of small focal length f_e. With the final image at infinity m = f_o/f_e and the tube length is f_o + f_e. A large objective aperture collects more light and improves resolution.

A concave mirror objective replaces the lens, so there is no chromatic aberration and the mirror can be supported over its whole back, allowing very large apertures. In the Cassegrain design a small convex secondary mirror returns the converging beam through a hole in the primary, giving a long effective focal length in a short tube.
